title: The door you left
hookLine: free, lost and guilty in one afternoon: leaving the religion you grew up in is common, the in-between has a name, and every door stays open

lines: A PEW, A MAT, A TABLE, A KITCHEN.
cards: Looking back can stir up an older door. Maybe you grew up with a pew, a prayer mat, a temple, a seder table, a gurdwara kitchen. And at some point you stepped out.
Maybe slowly. Maybe with a slam. Now the holidays feel strange, and some songs still catch in your throat.
You can feel free, and lost, and guilty, all in one afternoon. A lot of people find their way to a path like this one from exactly there. If that's you, you're not behind, and you're not alone.

teach.b: First, it's common. In a large American survey from 2015, about a third of adults said they now have a different religious identity from the one they were raised in. Second, what people feel.
Leaving can come with real grief: for a community, a calendar, the music, the sense of being held. Some people feel anger. Some feel guilt, or fear of being punished.
Family dinners can get tense. All of that is normal, and none of it proves you chose wrong, or right. Third, the in-between has a name.
In 1909 the folklorist Arnold van Gennep studied rites of passage around the world and found three stages: leaving, a threshold, and arriving.
He named the threshold stage from the Latin word for a doorway, limen. Later the anthropologist Victor Turner described people in that stage as betwixt and between. It's disorienting by design.
It's also where new things begin. Fourth, a promise this path makes.

teach.h: NO SIDE TO PICK. HELP IS THERE.
teach.b: It won't ask you to pick a side. Some people who leave a tradition return to it later, often in a new way. Some find another home.
Some stay in between for years. Each of those is welcome here, and none of the seven doors you visited this year has closed.
And if the lost feeling ever gets heavy, the kind where it's hard to see a reason to keep going, please tell someone today.
In the US you can call or text 988 at any hour, and wherever you are, local emergency help is there.

how: Rites of passage in many cultures move through leaving, a threshold and arriving; people who step away from a childhood tradition often spend a long time in that threshold, and many traditions welcome those who return.

o: a feeling hidden just below the edge of awareness
the last point before a person finally gives up
the in-between stage, on the threshold of a change

p: U.S. adults with a new religious identity

s: leaving the religion you grew up in is rare
a large 2015 U.S. survey found about a third of adults now have a different religious identity.
grief and guilt after leaving are common, and don't prove anything
they're normal parts of a passage, not a verdict.
once you leave a tradition, its door is closed
some people return, often in a new way; some find another home; some stay in between.

games.q: a friend who stopped going to services says the holidays now make them feel lost and guilty. what helps most?
o: tell them they should go back or get over it.
say it's a common in-between, and they don't have to decide anything today.
games.why: between is a place too. no side to pick, and if it ever gets heavy, help is there.

practice: If you left a tradition, or drifted from one, picture its door, the building, a smell, a sound, and notice what comes up: warmth, ache, anger, or nothing at all; all of it is allowed.
If you never had one, picture any threshold you've crossed: a move, a breakup, a new job. Breathe right there in the doorway; you don't have to step either way.

wordCard.voice: Liminal, from the Latin for doorway: the in-between stage of a passage. Disorienting, and where new things start. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: threshold, doorway; the root of liminal, van Gennep's word for the middle stage of a rite of passage.

carryVoice: Your line: between is a place too. You don't have to have arrived anywhere yet. Until tomorrow.
